When I rate a toll road, I do not start with the engineering. I start with three questions. First, how likely is the traffic forecast? Most forecasts are too optimistic, so I usually reduce them by twenty percent. Second, who has to pay if the costs go up? If the contract is clear, the risk is lower. If nobody knows, the concessionaire will probably pay, and that must affect the rating. Third, can the government change the tariff? In some countries, that is very unlikely. In others, it may happen before every election. The answer to those three questions decides most of the rating.

Good morning, everybody. Here is our risk update for the quarter. The good news is that none of our projects is close to a default. Traffic on the two toll roads is higher than we expected, and both concessionaires are creditworthy. The bad news is the currency. The dollar went up eight percent, and if it continues, our returns are likely to fall next year. We have to be honest about that. We are not going to sell anything in a panic. But we may need to hedge a larger part of the debt, and we will decide that at the next board meeting in March.
